India ranked among the top countries with the highest heatwave exposure for both vulnerable age groups — infants and older adults — along with China, the U.S. and Russia, according to the tenth indicator report of the Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change.
Globally, total number of heatwave days decreased from 2024's historical high of 15.3 billion person-days for older adults and 2.3 billion person-days for infants. The year 2025 was the second highest on record for heatwave exposure for both vulnerable groups combined as older adults were exposed to 10.8 billion person-days of heatwaves, while infants experienced 1.1 billion person-days, the report said.
Visual Story: How heat stressed are you?
When normalised by population size, older adults experienced on average 12.8 heatwave days per individual in 2025, while infants experienced on average 8.7 heatwave days per individual, it said.
Authors of the report, led by those at the U.K.'s University College London, said climate action is picking up around the world, but failing to keep pace with global warming, especially as health harms of climate change grew faster in the decade since the 2016 Paris Agreement, compared to the previous one.
A decade after the Paris Agreement, the report's authors are calling for climate change to be formally declared a global health emergency, for a new WHO instrument to enable a coordinated global response, and for governments to put health at the centre of every climate decision, from emissions targets to climate funding.

Priorities include urgent, fair cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, sustained investment in science, and climate finance for health delivered as grants rather than loans, so that countries can adapt without taking on more debt, they said.
"A decade after the Paris Agreement, our findings are unambiguous: the health harms of climate change are growing faster than the world's response to them, and in many cases even accelerating," author Marina Romanello, executive director of the Lancet Countdown, professor at University College London, said.
Real progress has been made in clean energy, health system readiness, and health-protective regulation, all of which are already delivering health benefits to local communities, Ms. Romanello said.
"However, progress has been too slow, too small, and isn't reaching those who need it most. That is why we are calling for climate change to be formally recognised as a global health emergency, with health placed at the centre of every climate decision," Ms. Romanello said.
Visual Story: How southwest monsoon deficit affected parts of India
In 2023 alone — the hottest year during 2016-2025 — heat was linked to a record 7,10,000 estimated deaths, exceeding those from malaria or HIV, with 71.5% of them driven by climate change.
Altogether, climate change is estimated to have caused almost 3 million heat deaths between 2016 and 2023, the authors said.

A group of 146 experts from more than 30 countries is calling for climate change to be officially declared a global health emergency after extreme heat caused a record number of deaths in 2023. The appeal appears in the latest Lancet Countdown report, coordinated by University College London and the World Health Organization and published ahead of the UN COP31 climate conference.
According to the report, extreme heat contributed to approximately 710,000 deaths in 2023, exceeding the annual death tolls associated with malaria or HIV. More than 70% of these deaths were attributed directly to human-caused warming. Between 2016 and 2023, nearly three million people died as a result of the effects of climate change.
The impact also extended to the economy. Heat-related productivity losses exceeded one trillion dollars annually over the past three years, while in 2025 severe drought affected nearly 52% of the planet’s land surface.
The experts are calling for a coordinated response from the WHO and for health to be integrated into all climate decisions. The report also notes progress, such as record investment in clean energy, but warns that it remains insufficient.

A new Lancet report reveals the growing toll of climate change on human health, from rising heat deaths and drought to food insecurity and lost livelihoods.
https://p.dw.com/p/5Oif2
Advertisement
As heat deaths, drought and food insecurity accelerate worldwide, nearly 150 researchers from more than 30 countries are calling for climate change to be declared a "global health emergency."
The health and economic toll of planetary heating has risen sharply in the decade since countries signed the Paris climate accord — a landmark deal to stop climate change that was hailed by the World Health Organization (WHO) at the time as "the most important public health agreement of the century."
Yet, climate change was responsible for more than half a million heat deaths in 2023 alone and nearly 3 million since 2016. The area affected by extreme drought, which threatens food and water supplies and raises the risk of disease, grew more than 700% faster than in the decade before. And heat cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion (around €962 billion) in lost potential income last year, all according to the annual Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change.
"This cannot continue," said Alan Dangour, director of climate and health at Wellcome Trust, one of the world's largest charities, which funded the Lancet report. "We must change course and put the health and well-being of people at the heart of our response to climate change — measuring success not through emissions targets or degrees Celsius but by lives saved and health outcomes improved."
Climate extremes are the new health threats — here is why
Climate-linked health harms growing faster than before
The latest findings from the Lancet study show how rapidly the health risks are growing by comparing this decade to the one before the Paris Agreement was signed.
Heat is the starkest example. Climate change was responsible for 68% of heat-related deaths between 2016 and 2023, up from 55% in the previous decade. The yearly increase in climate-driven heat deaths more than doubled over the same period.
But deaths are only "the tip of the iceberg," said Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney's Heat and Health Research Center. "Except that iceberg is not melting, it's growing every year." Beneath the surface are also heatstroke, lost sleep and worsening chronic health conditions.
Heat wiped out 573 billion potential working hours in 2025, with farmworkers bearing the brunt. Vulnerable economies in Africa and South-East Asia were hit hardest with losses reaching 5% of GDP, compared with 0.5% in the more developed economies.
"The economic toll is battering vulnerable sectors and communities the hardest," Marina Romanello, executive director of the Lancet Countdown, who is based at University College London, told journalists at a press briefing.
Water extremes are intensifying too. Satellite data show that since 2003, 43% of the world's land has been steadily drying out, while 37% has been getting wetter. Together, that is more than 80% of land shifting to extremes that threaten crops, food supplies and sanitation.
Why Europe's extreme summers are getting worse
Drought can leave people without safe drinking water and raises the risk of infectious disease, while floods bring drowning, injury and contaminated water.
Heat waves and droughts pushed nearly 128 million more people into food insecurity in 2024, compared with the 1981–2010 average.
"This isn't a gradual worsening; it's a step change," Romanello said.
What would declaring a global health emergency change?
To save lives and protect human health, experts are calling for a new WHO instrument to help countries share information, coordinate responses, monitor threats and disburse funds. The United Nations and its member states would create the mechanism.
The closest existing version of this is the WHO's Public Health Emergency of International Concern mechanism (PHEIC) used during the COVID-19 pandemic and mpox outbreaks. But built with short-term emergencies in mind, it falls short of addressing a complex threat that requires sustained global action across multiple sectors, like climate change.
The world needs a broader approach, "so that we're not responding to emergency after emergency," said Romanello. "We're doing a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies."
Progress happening but not nearly fast enough
Romanello told journalists that "we have more than enough proof" that such action does improve health outcomes. "Early warning systems informed by climate, have already seen a reduction in the adverse impacts of these extreme weather events," she said.
The growth in renewable energy has also partly aided a reduction in deaths from fossil fuel air pollution in half of 140 countries assessed since 2016, preventing an estimated 323,000 deaths a year.
And 56 countries now have national plans to adapt their health services for climate impacts, such as heat waves and disease outbreaks, up from just 14 in 2015.
But progress remains too slow, according to the report.
Fossil fuels, the burning of which releases emissions fueling planetary heating as well as other pollutants, still supply more than 80% of the world's energy.
Energy-related emissions hit a record high in 2024. The world's 100 largest oil and gas companies are on track to produce 150% more oil and gas by 2040 than is compatible with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit). A year ago, that figure was 138%.
Investing in an old technology
Governments continue to fund fossil fuels, with net subsidies doubling since 2016 to $6.2 trillion. In 2024, 10 countries spent more on such subsidies than on their entire health systems.
Yet as fossil fuel prices rise and renewables become cheaper, these polluting technologies are becoming increasingly uneconomical, said Romanello.
Romanello likened new fossil fuel investment to "investing in Blockbuster when you have Netflix," — a bet on an old technology, referring to the once ubiquitous video rental store that failed to adapt to streaming.
Meanwhile, money to help health systems adapt to climate change is scarce. Developing countries estimate they need around $3.3 billion a year for such adaptations, which the Lancet authors say is likely an underestimate. Only about a third of that was committed in 2024. Foreign aid reductions, led by the US and followed by Germany, which made the second-largest cut, are widening the gap.
"This report is a stark warning that climate change is a health emergency," said Helen Clark, former prime minister of New Zealand and chair of the Lancet Countdown's board. "What's missing is not evidence, but the political will to act on it."

Local government units (LGUs) should establish free drinking water stations and cooling centers to protect residents from extreme heat amid forecasts of a potentially strong El Niño, Sen. Risa Hontiveros said Tuesday.
Hontiveros urged LGUs to work with the national government to provide free drinking water through hydration stations to help prevent heat-related illnesses, including heat stroke.
“Dapat may libreng drinking water stations sa mga lugar kung saan araw-araw na nagtatrabaho at nagtitipon ang ating mga kababayan. Hindi dapat dagdag gastos ang pag-iwas sa dehydration at heat stroke (There should be free drinking water stations in places where our fellow Filipinos work and gather every day. She said monitoring and reporting heat index levels alone would not suffice, stressing the need to ensure public access to clean drinking water.
Hontiveros also suggested converting existing public spaces, such as schools, libraries, museums and community centers, into cooling shelters during periods of extreme heat.
Malls and other private establishments could likewise designate comfortable, air-conditioned common areas where people can rest and cool down without having to make a purchase, she added.
With experts projecting a potentially strong El Niño, Hontiveros stressed the need for both public and private sectors to prepare for its effects.
She said these measures are among the immediate solutions that could help mitigate the effects of the projected “Super El Niño.”
The Senate Ad Hoc Committee on Reinvigorating Investment and Sustainable Economic Growth, which Hontiveros also chairs, has been tasked with looking into measures to address the phenomenon’s anticipated effects. (PNA)

ERC exploring consumer relief measures as peso continues to weaken
October 28, 2026 | 8:46 pm
PHILSTAR FILE PHOTO
SINGAPORE — The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) said it is studying how to cushion the potential impact on consumers of rising electricity prices as the peso’s continued weakness makes imported fuel used by power plants more expensive.
“We are still studying what measures we can take to anticipate the increase in generation charges resulting from the depreciation of the peso,” ERC Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Francis Saturnino C. Juan said on Wednesday on the sidelines of the Singapore International Energy Week.
The peso closed at an all-time low of P64.17 per dollar on Tuesday, against the previous record low of P63.95 a day earlier, according to the Bankers Association of the Philippines.
This marked the peso’s 38th record low this year and its ninth so far in October.
As a net energy importer, the Philippines is exposed to higher fuel costs as the currency weakens, making imported energy resources, such as coal, natural gas, and diesel more expensive.
These higher costs could eventually be passed on to electricity consumers through their monthly bills.
Mr. Juan said legislators have asked the ERC to implement measures to mitigate the potential impact of peso deprecation on power rates.
He said the peso’s depreciation will not immediately show up in distribution charges, as these rates are determined through a rate reset process. Instead, the more immediate impact would be on power generation costs, which are passed on to consumers.
“The most immediate impact of foreign exchange movements would be on generation charge pass-throughs, given how generation prices are structured,” he said.
He said the relief measures currently in place include allowing staggered electricity bill payment and preventing disconnections due to unpaid bills.
Energy Secretary Sharon S. Garin has said that she plans to discuss with Mr. Juan measures to cushion the impact of higher costs arising from the weak peso.
“We have the oil crisis. We have the currency depreciation. We have the El Niño and the coming summer,” she said. “This is not the best time to be Energy Secretary, but we try as much as possible to minimize the impact.” — Sheldeen Joy Talavera
